analysis.one_liner: Lets governors veto federal endangered species listings and lets states take over species protection within their borders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a May 2015 hearing, it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that no species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of every governor in whose state it lives, and no listing would take effect until both chambers of Congress voted to approve it. Every listing would expire automatically after five years. States could take over protection of any species found only within their borders, and courts would be barred from reviewing those decisions. The bill also ends citizens' ability to petition for listings and to recover attorney fees in enforcement lawsuits, lets landowners' projects count as legal if the Interior Department misses a 90-day review deadline, and requires taxpayers to pay landowners 150% of a property's value when federal protection cuts its value by half.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and developers would gain the most: a 90-day silence rule would automatically approve proposed land uses, and payments of 150% of fair market value would compensate them when species protection significantly reduces a property's value. Agriculture, mining, timber, and energy interests would face fewer federal restrictions on land use. States would gain exclusive control over species found only within their borders, with no court review. Federal power administrations would have to itemize endangered-species compliance costs on customers' bills.

how_it_helps.text: No species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of the governor of each state where it is present, and no listing could take effect until Congress enacted a joint resolution approving it [S2].
Every approved listing would be automatically removed five years later, and could only return through another act of Congress, in consultation with the governors [S2].

A governor could take exclusive control of regulating any species found only within that state — including writing regulations, designating critical habitat, issuing permits, and running recovery plans — on all land in the state, and that action could not be reviewed by any federal or state court [S3].

Landowners could submit any proposed use of their property for a federal determination; if the Interior Department failed to respond within 90 days, the use would be deemed compliant, and that determination would be an affirmative defense to any penalty or prosecution [S3].

If a Fish and Wildlife Service action cut the fair market value of property by at least 50% for its intended use, taxpayers would pay the owner or lessee 150% of the property's fair market value within 180 days [S3].
The bill would eliminate the citizen petition process for adding or removing species from the lists and would strip the award of attorney fees in citizen enforcement suits under the Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the public would bear the cost: federal endangered species protections would depend on governors' and Congress's approval, listings would expire automatically, and citizens would lose their main tool for enforcing the law through the courts. Taxpayers would fund the 150% property-value compensation payments and the appraisals. Species found in only one state would depend entirely on that governor's willingness to protect them, with no court to check the decision.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weakened species protection and payouts

drawbacks.text: The bill responded to a real grievance: under current law landowners effectively bear the cost of conserving endangered species habitat on their own property, and the bill's findings state the Act penalizes them for it [S3]. The 150% compensation scheme was an attempt — albeit an expensive one — to shift that burden to taxpayers.

Supporters could argue the automatic five-year expiration would force periodic democratic reauthorization of listings, and that requiring compensation would give the government a financial incentive to use its regulatory power sparingly.

The costs were severe: eliminating judicial review of state takeover decisions, deeming unreviewed land uses legal after 90 days, and requiring a new act of Congress for every listing would have made protecting species with any commercial value nearly impossible, and taxpayers would fund large compensation payouts and appraisal costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine problem — landowners who bear conservation costs without compensation — but the cure went far past it. Between governor vetoes, mandatory congressional approval, five-year sunsets, a deemed-approved rule for land uses, court-proof state takeovers, and 150% compensation, the bill would have left the Endangered Species Act a shell, with taxpayers covering large payouts to property owners. Whatever accountability it added for regulators, it removed far more accountability for the regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which held one hearing in May 2015, and the committee never advanced it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on March 24, 2015, joined by one cosponsor, Senator Dean Heller [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
On May 6, 2015, the committee held a hearing on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 114-37 [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal endangered species protections and citizen enforcement tools stayed intact. Developers, extractive industries, and landowners who would have gained from governor vetoes, deemed-approved land uses, and 150% taxpayer-funded compensation got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Dean Heller
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator to do so.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held one hearing in May 2015, and never voted to report it out, keeping it off the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only Senate support was its two Republican sponsors, and the committee — where no member moved it forward — never brought it to a decision.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: A 90-day deemed-approved rule for land uses and 150% taxpayer-funded compensation for value reductions would remove the main federal check on developing habitat. The cost of that relief would fall on taxpayers and on species protection.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, timber, and other extractive industries
industries.note: Requiring governor consent and congressional approval for every listing, expiring listings after five years, and letting states take over single-state species would sharply limit federal regulation of their operations.
The bill's findings frame the Act as penalizing landowners for harboring species habitat; state control and compensation payments would lift federal restrictions from farm and ranch operations.
The bill eliminates the citizen petition process for listings and the award of attorney fees in citizen suits, removing the main levers these groups use to enforce the Act in court.

Governors would gain veto power over federal listings and exclusive authority over species found only in their state, with courts barred from reviewing those decisions — transferring a federal conservation duty to state political control.

industries.industry: Federal power administrations and their electricity customers
industries.note: The Bonneville, Southeastern, Southwestern, and Western power administrations would have to show customers on monthly bills their share of endangered species compliance costs, adding a reporting burden while giving ratepayers cost transparency.
